title: In vitro and in vivo growth alter the population dynamic and properties of a Jeryl Lynn mumps vaccine.
ehr_evidence: The study used no electronic health record data; data were generated from in vitro virus growth in Vero and MDCK cell lines, in vivo neonatal rat neurovirulence testing, plaque assays, Sanger and deep sequencing, and mass spectrometry.
summary: An in vitro and in vivo comparative laboratory study of two closely related Jeryl Lynn-5 mumps vaccine strains (JL-CK grown on primary canine kidney cells and RIT4385 grown on chicken embryo fibroblasts) showing that propagation in cell lines or neonatal rat brains dramatically alters the virus population dynamics and properties.
key_findings: JL-CK produced 100-fold more progeny virus than RIT4385 in Vero cells (p < 0.0001) and MDCK cells (p = 0.0365).
JL-CK plaques were at least three times smaller than RIT4385 plaques (p < 0.0001).
JL-CK had higher neurovirulence potential than RIT4385 in neonatal rats (p = 0.0035) but significantly less than the wild-type Mu90 (p < 0.001).
Sanger sequencing identified 14 regions of heterogeneity in JL-CK, and plaque purification revealed five distinct Jeryl Lynn-5 variants plus a parent-like variant at only 4% frequency.
K36R mutation increased 9.6-fold during in vivo growth in neonatal rat brains, indicating preferential selection of JL-CK1.
RIT4385 was more genetically stable than JL-CK across Vero and MDCK passage.
JL-CK5 grew slowest (max titre 1.46 × 10^6 pfu/ml at 5 d.p.i.) while JL-CK1 produced the highest titre (1.35 × 10^7 pfu/ml at 3 d.p.i.).
captured_features: Neurovirulence score (ventricle cross-sectional area as percentage of whole brain)
study_design: Comparative experimental in vitro and in vivo virology study
population: In vitro: Vero and MDCK cell lines; in vivo: neonatal rat pups (n = 9 per group, Mu90 n = 3)
exposure_domain: Vaccine production cell substrate / viral propagation in cell lines and animal tissue
limitations: Small animal group sizes used to minimise animal usage.
Significant variation in results between individual animals.
No established correlate of protection and no animal model mimicking human mumps disease.
Impact of genetic variation on vaccinated populations is not understood.
